title: Emit exactly one non-empty title element per page
statement: Every indexable HTML response contains one title element inside head whose text content is neither empty nor an unreplaced template placeholder, and no response contains a second title element.
rationale: The title element is the primary label a result listing has for a page, so when it is absent, empty, or duplicated the engine constructs a label from whatever other text it finds and the site loses control of how the page is named.
implementation: Locate the single layer that owns the document head for each route and set the title there. If the framework merges a layout title with a route title, confirm the merged result yields one element rather than one per layer, and remove any hardcoded fallback that survives into production.

verification.method: Count title elements in the head of the served response for a sample of routes and record the text content of each one found.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

title: Provide a single meta description per indexable page
statement: Each indexable page carries at most one meta description element, and where present its content describes that specific page rather than repeating a site-wide sentence across every route.
rationale: A description that is present and page-specific gives the engine a candidate snippet drawn from the page's own subject; a site-wide sentence gives it nothing to prefer over text it extracts from the body itself.
implementation: Set the description where the route already knows its own subject - the page module, the content record, or the CMS field - rather than in a shared layout default. Where no page-specific text exists, omit the element instead of emitting a generic one.

verification.method: Collect the description meta content from the served response across a route sample and count how many distinct values appear.

caution: Search engines frequently generate their own snippet in place of the supplied description, so this control makes a page-specific candidate available; it does not determine what is displayed.

sources.title: Control your snippets in search results

title: Declare the document primary language on the root html element
statement: The html element of every response carries a lang attribute holding a well-formed BCP 47 tag that names the language the page's main content is actually written in.
rationale: Assistive technology selects a pronunciation profile from this attribute and localization tooling uses it to decide which pages belong to which language, so an absent or wrong value degrades both without producing any visible error.
implementation: Set the attribute in the root document template. On a multilingual site, derive it from the same source of truth that selects the content locale rather than hardcoding one tag, and mark inline passages in another language with their own lang attribute.

verification.method: Read the lang attribute from the root element of each served response and compare the declared tag against the language of the page's main content.

sources.title: WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 3.1.1 Language of Page
HTML Standard: the lang and xml:lang attributes

title: Declare a mobile viewport in the document head
statement: Every response includes a viewport meta element that maps the layout viewport to the device width, so the page is laid out at the device's own width instead of a desktop default that is then scaled down.
rationale: Without the declaration a mobile browser assumes a desktop-width canvas and shrinks the result, which makes text and controls smaller than the platform's own mobile guidance expects.
implementation: Add the declaration to the root document template once. Before adding it to a site that has never had one, load the page at a narrow width and check the layout still works, because removing the desktop-scaling fallback changes rendering on every mobile visit.

verification.method: Read the viewport meta content from the served response and confirm the layout at a narrow viewport width does not overflow horizontally.

title: Give every indexable route a distinct title
statement: No two indexable routes share an identical title string, and templated titles interpolate a value that varies per route rather than only a constant site suffix.
rationale: Identical titles across routes leave nothing in the label to tell one result from another, and the engine has to fall back on page text to differentiate pages that the site itself failed to differentiate.
implementation: Build titles from the route's own primary subject plus at most one constant suffix. For collection and paginated routes, include the discriminator - page number, filter value, or locale - so the generated strings stay distinct rather than collapsing onto one value.

verification.method: Gather the title from every route in the route inventory, then group identical strings and report each group holding more than one route.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

title: Serve search-critical metadata in the initial server response
statement: The title, description, canonical, and robots directives are present in the response body as it leaves the server, not injected later by client-side script after the document has loaded.
rationale: Directives that only appear after script execution are absent from the first fetch, and any consumer that reads the response without running the page's JavaScript sees a document with no metadata at all.
implementation: Move metadata resolution into whichever server phase already produces the document shell - the framework's head API, a server route handler, or the prerender step. Do not keep a client-side fallback that writes the same tags again, because two writers produce duplicate elements.

verification.method: Fetch the route without executing JavaScript and diff the metadata elements found there against the same elements in the rendered document.
